ABSTRACT

This research focuses on optimizing Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS) for cost reduction. The methodology enhances the loading process by applying advanced algorithms and metaheuristics to identify optimal locations for each Stock Keeping Unit (SKU).

One of the central issues we address in this study is the Container Loading Problem (CLP), an NP-Hard problem that has persisted for many years. The approach undertaken here is twofold: firstly,  to  maximize  space  utilization,  thereby  reducing  the  wastage  of  slots,  and  secondly,  to strategically  assign locations for  each SKU based on the overall order quantity. This two-step methodology enables us to calculate the total number of PODs (Portable On Demand storage units) required for efficient operations.

This  research  was  conducted  by  incorporating  real-world  observations  and  adjusting empirical data to simulate a practical context for our experiment. This experiment's constraints also reflect real-world limitations, including the direction of rotation and the restriction against placing  different  SKUs  in  the  same  slot.  These  factors  make  our  study  more  reflective  of  the challenges faced in warehouse environments.

This  research  demonstrates  that  our  method  effectively  identifies  the  accurate  number  of PODs required to fulfill the order requirements, thus helping warehouses minimize the cost of surplus  POD  placements.  By  providing  a  means  to  anticipate  the  required  number  of  PODs accurately, our study contributes to the wider discourse on improving warehouse efficiency and decreasing operational costs. We believe these insights and the associated strategies presented here can be a valuable resource for businesses looking to optimize their RMFS operations and achieve significant cost reductions.

1.1 Background

With  the  rapid  growth  of  e-commerce  and  online  shopping,  there  has  been  an  increasing demand for efficient and automated order fulfillment systems. According to analysts, the global ecommerce share of retail sales is predicted to  grow this  year  and reach  20.8%. By 2026, it is forecasted to increase by 5.2 percentage points to 24%, indicating significant growth in just six years [1]. Hence, conventional transportation methods are inadequate, and adopting automated and efficient means of retrieving and transporting goods is imperative. Achieving automation in the warehouse plays a vital role in attaining optimal levels of automation and autonomy, which leads to faster, safer, and more efficient day-to-day operations. By leveraging automated processes in the warehouse, costs are reduced, and delivery times are improved, resulting in a leaner, more scalable, and eco-friendly operation [2].

Implementing  automation  in  order-picking  is  possible  by  utilizing  the  Robotic  Mobile Fulfillment System (RMFS), a semi-automated parts-to-picker system commonly employed in ecommerce  warehouses.  This  system  employs  an  automatic  guided  vehicle  (AGV)  to  convey movable  shelves(pods)  to  the  designated  picking  stations,  facilitating  the  automation  process. Despite  advancements  in  the  implementation  of  this  system,  there  are  several  distinct  actions carried  out  by  different  entities  at  various  phases  of  the  robot  routing  problem  [3],  product assignment, pod storage allocation [4], layout design [5], and AGV energy consumption [6]. The task of executing RMFS is a laborious undertaking that involves numerous intricate subproblems. Without proper management, the RMFS cannot run the warehouse smoothly. Therefore, many studies have been working on RMFS [7]. Yang, Jin [8] Conducted a study that analyzed the effect of warehouse configuration on the throughput. They analyzed some factors, including lane depth, number of aisles, picking stations, and robots. Yang and Hua [9] optimize robot utilization by designing a policy for order sequencing  and rack scheduling.  Keung,  Lee [10] focuses on the charging  assignment  problem.  Some  recent  studies  focus  on  pick  order  and  pod  assignment, including [11, 12].
Among all problems in RMFS, one problem that also might influence the efficiency of the warehouse is the item-to-pod allocation problem. While most of the studies focus on pod allocation

and  pod  selection  based  on  demand,  very  limited  studies  discuss  the  item-to-pod  assignment, which also considers the dimension of the items. An optimal item assignment to the pods might reduce the pods required to fulfill the demand. Thus, it can reduce the cost of pod investment, the size of the storage area in the warehouse, and the overall warehouse operational cost. Therefore, this study aims to improve pod utilization by optimizing the item-to-pod assignment.

The  item-to-pod  assignment  problem  is  similar  to  the  three-dimensional  (3D)  bin-packing problem. The 3D bin packing problem, an extension of the one-dimensional and two-dimensional problems, is crucial in logistics planning. It is ubiquitous in the real world, encompassing steel, textiles,  transportation,  and  manufacturing industries.  It  aims to increase  the utilization rate of trucks or containers to enhance system efficiency. In this study, the 3D bin-packing problem is applied in RMFS to reduce the extra costs caused by the need for multiple shelves due to inefficient warehouse shelf space utilization.

The  Bin  Packing  Problem  (BPP)  is  one  of  the  most  famous  problems  in  combinatorial optimization  problems  that  manifest  in  numerous  practical  applications  within  the  fields  of transportation and logistics. According to the improved typology of Wäscher, Haußner [13], BPP has been studied since the 1970s [14, 15]. However,  the implementation of BPP in RMFS is still rare. A similar problem with BPP is the container loading problem (CLP). Both BPP and CLP are categorized as NP-hard problems. Until recent years, there has been research proposing the use of deep learning to solve such problems. However, heuristic algorithms remain the most favored by many. Hajlaoui and Jaoua [16] present a new Reinforcement Learning model for container loading. It performs well and shows that lower training variability yields better results than high training variability. Kurpel and Scarpin [17] offer new, effective solutions for container loading problems, considering conditions like box orientation, load stability, and separation of boxes. Zhang, Gu [18] introduces a new hybrid heuristic algorithm to address the container loading problem efficiently. Gajda, Trivella [19] introduces a new heuristic algorithm to solve a complex logistics problem, balancing cargo value and multiple constraints.

A pod  in  RMFS  consists  of  several  slots.  The  slots  can  have  the  same  or  different  sizes. Maximizing the number of items stored in a slot is similar to the 3D bin packing problem. This study proposes a heuristics algorithm to design the item's arrangement in a slot to optimize the slot's utilization. Furthermore, because there are many different slots and pods, the next problem is which item should be stored in which slot in which pod. This problem is a combinatorial problem.
Therefore, this study applies a metaheuristics approach to solve this problem. Regarding algorithm selection, we adopted GA and PSO, which have been widely used [20-23], as our methodologies.
1.2 Objectives

This study aims to optimize pod utilization by maximizing the number of items stored in each slot  and  finding  the  best  item-slot-pod  arrangement.  This  study  combines  heuristics  and metaheuristics  algorithms  to  find  the  optimal  solution.  This  study  applies  two  metaheuristics algorithms: particle swarm optimization (PSO) and genetic algorithm (GA).

CHAPTER 2
LITERATURE REVIEW
2.1 Robotic Mobile Fulfillment System

In  numerous  warehouses,  products  or  items  are  traditionally  stacked  on  shelves  in  an organized manner to facilitate retrieval, and personnel, often referred to as pickers, actively pick and pack these items according to specific customer orders. In situations with an intense flux of goods moving in and out of the warehouse, which is common in large-scale operations, Automated Storage/Retrieval Systems (AS/RS) are widely employed to streamline the process and enhance efficiency. However, this conventional warehouse automation method has limitations, including a rigid structure that makes altering inventory locations cumbersome, relatively high initial setup costs, and manual intervention in reallocating resources.

To combat these inherent challenges and to revolutionize the warehousing industry, Robotic Mobile  Fulfillment  Systems  (RMFS)  have  been  introduced  as  an  innovative  solution.  RMFS, characterized by its integration of cutting-edge robotics, is tailor-made for the unique demands of e-commerce warehouses. At the core of the RMFS is an automated parts-to-picker system. This system employs autonomous robots that tirelessly transport movable shelves, aptly termed 'pods,' to  and  fro  between storage areas and workstations. This system's ingenuity lies in eliminating walking time for pickers, which is achieved by having the pods brought directly to them. This process dramatically increases the picking rate, thereby enhancing overall productivity.

Within the workstations, there is a hive of activity where inventory is methodically placed onto the pods or diligently retrieved from them based on the requirements of the order at hand. Nevertheless,  implementing  RMFS  has  complexities  and  challenges    [24].  Notably,  logistical issues  include  the  strategic  assignment  of  customer  orders  to  workstations  and  the  efficient allocation of pods to storage locations [25]. These decision-making processes are not trivial and require intricate trade-offs to optimize the system. For instance, it might be logical to prioritize an order nearing its deadline by assigning it to a workstation. However, synergizing it with another order that shares a common aisle with the orders assigned to that workstation could lead to more efficient picking strategies. This condition might entail more picks per pod, reducing the trips each pod  needs  to  make,  culminating  in  enhanced  efficiency  and  resource  optimization.  The implementation of RMFS, therefore, necessitates careful planning and intelligent decision-making to harness its potential fully [26].

Based on past research [11, 27-29], there is a plethora of literature concerning the placement of SKUs in pods. Some studies have considered factors such as the association of SKU locations, the correlation in picking, batch processing, and the distance to move to other sites. Additionally, heuristic algorithms have been proposed to minimize inventory costs as much as possible. This study integrates the CLP with this issue and employs heuristic algorithms to enhance the efficiency of solving the problem.
2.2 Container loading problem

The CLP is a geometric assignment challenge that entails loading a subset of rectangular items, often denoted as SKU (Stock Keeping Units), into a fixed-dimension rectangular container, such as pods. The aim is to maximize the volume of the packed boxes. The packing process has to satisfy an optimized objective function under two primary geometric feasibility prerequisites:

CLP  are  diverse,  with  various  properties  constituting  their  characteristics.  They are traditionally categorized into two groups, as outlined by Wäscher and Haußner [13]. In the input minimization problem, the first category assumes sufficient storage space for all boxes. In such cases,  the  number of  containers  is  usually  non-restrictive,  with  the  primary  objective  being  to minimize the number of containers required to accommodate all boxes. Conversely, the second group,  the  output  maximization  problem,  operates  under  limited  container  space,  which  is insufficient for storing  all boxes. The aim here is to select a subset of boxes to maximize the volume or value of the load.

The classifications of cutting and packing problems proposed by Dyckhoff [30] and Wäscher, Haußner  [13]  offer  solid  foundations  for  investigations  in  this  field.  According  to  Wäscher, Haußner [13], these problems can be grouped based on dimensionality, the variety of large and small  items,  and  the  objective.  Within  the  scope  of  this  paper,  the  focus  is  primarily  on  3D rectangular items, with discussions on both single-bin and multi-bin packing problems.
2.2.1 Single bin packing problem

The single-bin packing problem is a classic cutting and packing problem, where the objective is to place a set of items into the minimum number of bins of fixed dimensions. Each item has a certain volume or weight, while each bin has a maximum capacity. The challenge lies in allocating the items into the bins to maximize space utilization. Most of the literature concerning packing problems focuses on this type of problem, and there are various adaptations based on different problem  descriptions,  including  the  development  of  corresponding  mathematical  models  and algorithms (Phongmoo, Leksakul [31] and Araya, Guerrero [32])
2.2.2 Multiple bin packing problem

The multi-bin packing problem extends the single-bin packing problem, where items can be divided into multiple categories or sets. Items from each set need to be packed into the same bin, and each bin can only contain items from a single set. Compared to the single-bin scenario, the multi-bin problem has received less attention. The objective is to satisfy the items' requirements with  the  minimum  number  of  containers.  In  past  literature,  Alonso  and  Alvarez-Valdes  [33] addressed this issue by minimizing the number of trucks used and solving it through an integer linear model while complying with certain constraints.
Ideally, we want to use the fewest shelves and have each slot filled as completely as possible. However, these two objectives may conflict in practice and must be balanced appropriately.
2.3 Common Solutions in the Past

The CLP is a complex combinatorial problem. Research on it has been steadily increasing over the past decades. In most studies, heuristic or metaheuristic methods are applied to solve this problem, although exact algorithms are also available. Heuristic methods provide solutions quickly and are effective for problems demanding real-time decisions or when computational resources are limited. The simplicity of heuristics contributes to their accessibility and ease of understanding. However, these methods, designed specifically for a problem, may not always find the optimal solution, and their performance can significantly vary depending on the problem instance. Huang and Hwang [34] propose a heuristic algorithm for resolving the three-dimensional single-container loading problem through optimal placement. Owing to the NP-hard nature of the problem, it is framed  as  a  zero-one  mixed  integer  linear  programming  model.  The  suggested  heuristic  has demonstrated superior efficiency to the cutting-edge mixed integer linear program and pre-existing heuristic approaches. Gajda, Trivella [19] proposed Randomized Constructive Heuristic (RCH) algorithm  quickly  generates  superior  packing  solutions  and  effectively  addresses  a  logistics company's CPL.

On  the  other hand, exact algorithms  guarantee  solutions'  optimality,  given  enough computational time. They provide a reliable and precise way to benchmark the quality of heuristic and  metaheuristic  solutions.  However,  their  main  limitation  is  computational  inefficiency  for large-scale  problems  due  to  their  exhaustive  nature,  making  them  impractical  for  real-time decision-making or problems with large dimensions. Martello and Pisinger [35] offered an exact branch-and-bound  method  to  find  optimal  solutions  for  small-scale  instances  of  the  threedimensional bin packing problem (3D-BPP). Although exact algorithms ensure optimal solutions, their applicability is constrained for cases involving many boxes.

Metaheuristics, being more general, offer flexibility in application across various problem domains. They tend to explore a broader search space and can often provide good-quality solutions, even for complex problems. However, they require careful tuning of parameters for each problem, and  there  is  no  guarantee  of  finding  an  optimal  solution.  Kurpel  and  Scarpin  [17]  introduce mathematical models for various container loading problems, evaluate box placement techniques, and propose new methods to set boundaries for input minimization issues. It uses well-known datasets for computational experiments, often achieving new or improved optimal solutions.

Metaheuristics,  adaptable  to  various  problems,  have  also  been  employed  in  tackling  the Container  Loading  Problem  (CLP),  in  contrast  to  heuristics,  which  are  tailored  for  specific problems. Adapting these metaheuristics necessitates modifications to accommodate  the representation  of  CLP  solutions.  The  roster  of  employed  metaheuristics  encompasses  Genetic Algorithms (GA) [20-23], PSO, Artificial Bee Colony Optimization [36], Tabu Search [37], and Simulated Annealing, among others.

This study addresses a Single Large Object Placement Problem (SLOPP), striving to place small  items  (SKUs)  into  containers  (Pods).  Given  various  Pod  sizes,  this  study  utilizes  a metaheuristic approach to identify the most appropriate placement for each SKU. Ultimately, the objective is to fulfill the same amount of order requirements with the minimum number of shelves.
2.4 Metaheuristics

Metaheuristics have found significant applicability in Container Loading Problems (CLPs) due  to  their  flexibility,  adaptability,  and  effectiveness  in  handling  complex  combinatorial optimization  issues.  As  CLPs  are  NP-hard,  signifying  inherent  computational  complexity intensifying  with  problem  size,  finding  optimal  solutions  for  large-scale  problems  becomes challenging. This condition paves the way for heuristic and metaheuristic methods. With their high adaptability,  metaheuristics  can  accommodate  various  optimization  problems,  including  CLPs. Their stochastic processes help avoid premature convergence and encourage a broader solution to space  exploration.  Balancing  between  exploring  new  solution  areas  and  intensively  searching promising ones, they efficiently generate near-optimal solutions within reasonable timeframes. Although they do not guarantee an optimal solution, their delivery of high-quality solutions makes them crucial in efficiently solving CLPs.

CHAPTER 3 METHODOLOGY

This section discusses the research methodology of this study. In the first step, this study represents the problem as a mathematical model to get a better problem definition. Furthermore, as the problem can be divided into two main problems, the item-to-slot arrangement, and SKU-topod assignment problems, this study solves each problem with different approaches. The item-toslot arrangement problem is how to arrange the items into a slot so that the number of items stored in a slot can be maximized. This problem is similar to a 3D CLP. This study solves this problem with a heuristics approach. Figure 3.1 represents the flowchart of the execution process in this study.

Besides optimizing the item's arrangement in a slot, finding the best SKU-to-pod assignment is also crucial to minimize the number of pods. As this problem is a combinatorial problem, this study utilizes genetic algorithms and particle swarm optimization algorithms to find the best SKUto-pod assignment.

3.1 Dimensionality Reduction with DBSCAN Clustering

DBSCAN stands for Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise [38]. It is particularly valued for its capability to detect clusters of arbitrary shapes, based on the density of data points, without specifying the number of clusters beforehand.

The algorithm employs two parameters, eps representing the maximum distance between two data points to be considered neighbors and min_samples, indicating the minimum number of points required to form a dense region. DBSCAN classifies points as core, border, or noise, with core points forming the clusters [38].

DBSCAN's ability to identify clusters of different shapes and handle noise efficiently has led to its widespread application in diverse fields like astronomy2 and bioinformatics [39]. However, the choice of parameters can significantly impact the results, and DBSCAN may struggle with clusters of varying densities.

This study will use this method to categorize thousands of SKUs (Stock Keeping Units) to reduce operational complexity. Moreover, items with large volumes are unlikely to be placed in the same pod. We have considered this issue and aim to distinguish SKUs through clustering.
3.2 Mathematical Formulation for the CLP

The item-to-pod arrangement or assignment can be represented as an extension of 3D CLP. This study defines this problem's main objective as minimizing the number of pods that serve all demands. In order to minimize the number of pods, the utilization of each slot in each pod should be maximized. Therefore, the first problem represented in the mathematical model is the items' arrangement in a slot to maximize the slots' utilization.
This study adopts a 3D cartesian coordinate system, with the left-bottom-back vertex as the origin point, as shown in Figure 3.2. The items are arranged orthogonally within the container.

In this section, we reference previous literature concerning the mathematical models of 3DCLP,  from  which  we  have  collated  the  relevant  mathematical  expressions  for  the  problem presented in this study.

elements.section_title: 3.4 Application of Genetic Algorithm in CLP
elements.text: This study employs a Genetic Algorithm (GA) to solve the SKU-to-pod assignment problem. The solution of SKU-to-pod assignment is the allocation of each SKU to available slots in all pods. Therefore,  this  study  represents  a  set  of  pods  with  several  slots  as  a  chromosome.  Each  pod represents a gene. Inside each gene, there are slots. For example, the chromosome would contain ten genes if a warehouse had ten pods, each with nine slots, as shown in Figure 3.6.

elements.section_title: 3.4 Application of Genetic Algorithm in CLP
elements.text: Because two main decisions should be encountered in the chromosome, each gene comprises two parts. elements.section_title: 3.5 Application of Particle Swarm Optimization in CLP
elements.text: The second algorithm employed in this study is the PSO algorithm. While the GA algorithm represents the SKU-to-Pod assignment as a chromosome, PSO represents it as a particle with the same  configuration  as  the  chromosome.  Drawing  parallels  to  the  Genetic  Algorithm  (GA) principles,  each  particle  undergoes  updates  influenced  by  the  particle's  optimal  historical movement and the optimal movement observed within the entire swarm. Let P be a set of particles, 𝑃 = {𝑝1, 𝑝 2 , … , 𝑝 𝑁 } ,  where N is the number of particles. The set P denotes the position of the particles, 𝑉 = {𝑣1, 𝑣 2 , … , 𝑣 𝑁 } represents the velocity of each particle's movement, and the final position of a particle equates to the solution. With each iteration, particles are updated continuously according to Equations ( 3-18 ) and ( 3-19 ). The particles traverse the search space through the formula,  gravitating  toward  their  best  and  globally  optimal  solutions.  This  strategy  assists  the particles in evading local optima and converging towards the global optimum.

elements.section_title: 3.5 Application of Particle Swarm Optimization in CLP
elements.text: The expressions 𝑃𝑏𝑒𝑠𝑡 𝑖 and 𝐺𝑏𝑒𝑠𝑡, respectively, signify the optimal position of an individual particle and the optimal position within the entire swarm. Three distinct parameters have been designated: w represents the inertia weight, while 𝑐1 and 𝑐2 are the cognitive and social learning factors. 𝑟 1 and 𝑟 2 are randomly generated numbers between 0 and 1 that are produced anew for every  particle  during  each  iteration.  The  process  of  updating  all  particles  continues  until  the established termination conditions are fulfilled.

3.6 Evaluating and Validating Fitness

We  evaluate  whether  the  solution  adheres  to  the  set  conditions  upon  executing  the metaheuristics. In our problem scenario, we demand that a certain quantity of each SKU be placed within the POD. Consequently, if each SKU fulfills the stipulated quantity, that solution is deemed feasible. If it does not, we identify the SKUs that have been excessively placed and not adequately placed and make substitutions until the condition is met. However, if there are no excessively placed SKUs, we will continue to add an empty POD and keep placing the unsatisfied SKUs until the  conditions  are  met. CHAPTER 4
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

The item-to-slot arrangement and SKU-to-pod assignment discussed in this study are the basic problems in RMFS. Thus, any warehouse implementing the RMFS must face this problem. This study also implements the proposed methods for a real case problem from a warehouse in Taiwan. However, before the real problem is implemented, the proposed method is evaluated using some artificial datasets. For the evaluation, the use of appropriate benchmark problems is critical for  evaluating  the  proposed  solutions.  Essentially,  such  experiments  can  be  divided  into benchmark instances and testbeds.

This section elucidates the computational outcomes for the suggested algorithms. For this study, all the proposed algorithms were formulated using Python 3.11.2 programming language and were executed on a personal computer equipped with an Intel Core i5-9400 processor and 16 GB RAM. The comprehensive experimental findings are discussed in the following subsections.
4.1 Data description

Our dataset comprises 5,729 distinct SKUs and three different types of PODs. Each POD has a varying number of SLOTs and sizes. To simplify the complexity of the experiments, we selected one of the POD types to address our research objectives. We further divided the SKU dataset into seven categories based on the degree of variation and quantity. These are categorized into strong, medium, and weak heterogeneity and differences in demand following the Poisson distribution.

This study adopts a multivariate approach to investigate how various parameter settings play a role in the simulations. The simulations systematically test different combinations of parameters to ensure a comprehensive analysis of how parameter configurations affect the outcomes. There are thirty runs for each set of parameter settings. This approach can mitigate the impact of random errors and observe with greater precision the variations in outcomes brought about by parameter changes. Table 4.7 to Table 4.12 summarize some of the experimental results. These tables display the result data under different parameter settings and reveal which parameters play a critical role in  the  simulations.  With  these  results,  decision-makers  can  make  more  informed  choices  of parameter settings for practical applications. By understanding the impact of various parameters, decision-makers can adjust the parameters based on specific objectives and needs. Furthermore, it is worth mentioning that although the results of this study provide valuable insights, the optimal choice of parameter settings may be influenced by different scenarios and conditions. Therefore, it is recommended to conduct further sensitivity analyses when applying these parameter settings to specific situations in order to ensure their applicability and effectiveness.

4.5 Real case study

This study aims to verify the feasibility of the proposed method by applying it to a practical problem. Based on our observations, the dataset in this study is adjusted from actual problem data. This problem hopes to effectively place order quantities within a given time frame onto PODs, using  the  minimum  number  of  PODs  to  satisfy  all  SKUs.  In  addition,  each  SLOT  can  only accommodate one type of SKU; different SKUs cannot be placed in the same SLOT. By applying the heuristic algorithm ensemble proposed in this study to this practical case, we find the minimum number of PODs required for the problem. Based on the previous section, it was concluded that parameter changes will significantly influence the experimental results. Therefore, the experiment was carried out with the optimal combination of parameters obtained. The parameter configuration for GA was set with a crossover rate of 0.7 and a mutation rate of 0.1. The parameter configuration for PSO, c1, c2, and w, were set at 1, 1, and 0.6, respectively. The results from the experiment showed that PSO could find a solution that met the conditions with fewer PODs used, but it also required more time.
5.1 Conclusion

In the ever-changing landscape of consumer behavior, e-commerce entities find themselves in a state of perpetual evolution, constantly seeking advancements and improvements. Central to their mission is a dual objective - curbing process and demand costs while satisfying customer needs. A crucial element of this mission involves a logistical challenge: determining the optimal quantity of pods required within the constraints of limited warehouse space.

Therefore, to tackle this challenge, various strategies must be considered: effective placement of stock in slots, the appropriate designation of location for each Stock Keeping Unit (SKU), and many more. Our study embraces the reality of these operational complexities and contributes a proposed  solution.  By  leveraging  a  novel  3D-CLP  algorithm  and  harnessing  the  power  of metaheuristics, we have devised a solution tailored to these intricate real-world problems.

In the context of this study, it is noteworthy that our focus is on the 3D CLP. Attempting to express the complexities of this problem through a conventional mathematical model would prove overly complex and demand a significant time investment. To bypass these hurdles, we adopt a heuristic approach. Our strategy zeroes in on SKU placement in slots, aiming for optimal space utilization.

Building  on  this,  we  employ  a  sinlge  objective  heuristic  approach  to  discern  the  ideal placement for each SKU. We aim to reduce the number of pods required to meet our operational objectives.

The  experimental  results  underscore  the  considerable  impact  of  parameter  changes.  Our experiment incorporated six distinct scenarios, characterized by different levels of heterogeneity strong, medium, and weak - and differences in quantities, specifically low and high demand. The best average pod needed in these scenarios was quantified as 10.90, 30.10, 13.10, 39.40, 19.00, and 103.30, respectively, which all the best average results obtained by using PSO.

An interesting pattern emerged when comparing the performance of GA and PSO in these scenarios.  Despite  the  longer  time  commitment  necessitated  by  PSO,  it  consistently  yielded superior results. This result reinforces the merit of investing more time upfront to derive more efficient and optimal outcomes.
CHAPTER 5
CONCLUSION & FUTURE WORK
5.2 Future Research

In the intricate realm of Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS), the dynamics of every operation hold paramount  significance. Each  action, whether latent or swift, can send reverberations throughout the system, instigating a chain reaction of effects on the subsequent tasks. In such a tightly-knit environment, even a slight deviation in one area can echo across the entire ecosystem, emphasizing the delicate interplay of components. A holistic approach becomes essential in a world where isolated solutions often fall short.

Our current study is grounded in real-world scenarios, drawing heavily from conditions typical to the Picking area. However, the breadth and depth of the RMFS world mean that our model, though  robust,  has  ample  room  for  expansion  and  further  fine-tuning.  The  more  nuances  we incorporate, the closer our model aligns with on-ground realities.

Stock allocation within the PODs  is far from a straightforward task.  Fundamental considerations, such as the weight-bearing capacity of each POD, must be juxtaposed against the collective endurance of the RMFS. It is a balancing act, ensuring we utilize the system to its fullest potential without overburdening it. Similarly, the strategic placement of stock is not just about space optimization but also about understanding the interrelationships between different Stock Keeping Units (SKUs). By analyzing buying patterns and SKU compatibility, we can create a layout where frequently co-purchased items are in proximity, streamlining retrieval processes and enhancing operational efficiency.

Central to our approach is the multi-objective heuristic algorithms, which, in their current form, represent just the tip of the iceberg. The possibilities are vast: from refining these algorithms to overhauling their architecture, every tweak can lead to substantial gains in computational speed. In doing so, we can pave the way for more agile, real-time solutions that resonate even more with the challenges of real-world RMFS. These enhancements can enrich the proposed model, bringing it closer to addressing the multifaceted challenges encountered in real-world RMFS.

This research focuses on optimizing Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS) for cost reduction. The methodology enhances the loading process by applying advanced algorithms and metaheuristics to identify optimal locations for each Stock Keeping Unit (SKU).
One of the central issues we address in this study is the Container Loading Problem (CLP), an NP-Hard problem that has persisted for many years. The approach undertaken here is twofold: firstly,  to  maximize  space  utilization,  thereby  reducing  the  wastage  of  slots,  and  secondly,  to strategically  assign locations for  each SKU based on the overall order quantity. This two-step methodology enables us to calculate the total number of PODs (Portable On Demand storage units) required for efficient operations.
This  research  was  conducted  by  incorporating  real-world  observations  and  adjusting empirical data to simulate a practical context for our experiment. This experiment's constraints also reflect real-world limitations, including the direction of rotation and the restriction against placing  different  SKUs  in  the  same  slot.  These  factors  make  our  study  more  reflective  of  the challenges faced in warehouse environments.

This  research  demonstrates  that  our  method  effectively  identifies  the  accurate  number  of PODs required to fulfill the order requirements, thus helping warehouses minimize the cost of surplus  POD  placements.  By  providing  a  means  to  anticipate  the  required  number  of  PODs accurately, our study contributes to the wider discourse on improving warehouse efficiency and decreasing operational costs. We believe these insights and the associated strategies presented here can be a valuable resource for businesses looking to optimize their RMFS operations and achieve significant cost reductions.

With  the  rapid  growth  of  e-commerce  and  online  shopping,  there  has  been  an  increasing demand for efficient and automated order fulfillment systems. According to analysts, the global ecommerce share of retail sales is predicted to  grow this  year  and reach  20.8%. By 2026, it is forecasted to increase by 5.2 percentage points to 24%, indicating significant growth in just six years [1]. Hence, conventional transportation methods are inadequate, and adopting automated and efficient means of retrieving and transporting goods is imperative. Achieving automation in the warehouse plays a vital role in attaining optimal levels of automation and autonomy, which leads to faster, safer, and more efficient day-to-day operations. By leveraging automated processes in the warehouse, costs are reduced, and delivery times are improved, resulting in a leaner, more scalable, and eco-friendly operation [2].

Implementing  automation  in  order-picking  is  possible  by  utilizing  the  Robotic  Mobile Fulfillment System (RMFS), a semi-automated parts-to-picker system commonly employed in ecommerce  warehouses.  This  system  employs  an  automatic  guided  vehicle  (AGV)  to  convey movable  shelves(pods)  to  the  designated  picking  stations,  facilitating  the  automation  process. Despite  advancements  in  the  implementation  of  this  system,  there  are  several  distinct  actions carried  out  by  different  entities  at  various  phases  of  the  robot  routing  problem  [3],  product assignment, pod storage allocation [4], layout design [5], and AGV energy consumption [6]. The task of executing RMFS is a laborious undertaking that involves numerous intricate subproblems. Without proper management, the RMFS cannot run the warehouse smoothly. Therefore, many studies have been working on RMFS [7]. Yang, Jin [8] Conducted a study that analyzed the effect of warehouse configuration on the throughput. They analyzed some factors, including lane depth, number of aisles, picking stations, and robots. Yang and Hua [9] optimize robot utilization by designing a policy for order sequencing  and rack scheduling.  Keung,  Lee [10] focuses on the charging  assignment  problem.  Some  recent  studies

focus  on  pick  order  and  pod  assignment, including [11, 12].
Among all problems in RMFS, one problem that also might influence the efficiency of the warehouse is the item-to-pod allocation problem. While most of the studies focus on pod allocation

and  pod  selection  based  on  demand,  very  limited  studies  discuss  the  item-to-pod  assignment, which also considers the dimension of the items. An optimal item assignment to the pods might reduce the pods required to fulfill the demand. Thus, it can reduce the cost of pod investment, the size of the storage area in the warehouse, and the overall warehouse operational cost. Therefore, this study aims to improve pod utilization by optimizing the item-to-pod assignment.
The  item-to-pod  assignment  problem  is  similar  to  the  three-dimensional  (3D)  bin-packing problem. The 3D bin packing problem, an extension of the one-dimensional and two-dimensional problems, is crucial in logistics planning. It is ubiquitous in the real world, encompassing steel, textiles,  transportation,  and  manufacturing industries.  It  aims to increase  the utilization rate of trucks or containers to enhance system efficiency. In this study, the 3D bin-packing problem is applied in RMFS to reduce the extra costs caused by the need for multiple shelves due to inefficient warehouse shelf space utilization.

The  Bin  Packing  Problem  (BPP)  is  one  of  the  most  famous  problems  in  combinatorial optimization  problems  that  manifest  in  numerous  practical  applications  within  the  fields  of transportation and logistics. According to the improved typology of Wäscher, Haußner [13], BPP has been studied since the 1970s [14, 15]. However,

the implementation of BPP in RMFS is still rare. A similar problem with BPP is the container loading problem (CLP). Both BPP and CLP are categorized as NP-hard problems. Until recent years, there has been research proposing the use of deep learning to solve such problems. However, heuristic algorithms remain the most favored by many. Hajlaoui and Jaoua [16] present a new Reinforcement Learning model for container loading. It performs well and shows that lower training variability yields better results than high training variability. Kurpel and Scarpin [17] offer new, effective solutions for container loading problems, considering conditions like box orientation, load stability, and separation of boxes. Zhang, Gu [18] introduces a new hybrid heuristic algorithm to address the container loading problem efficiently. Gajda, Trivella [19] introduces a new heuristic algorithm to solve a complex logistics problem, balancing cargo value and multiple constraints.

A pod  in  RMFS  consists  of  several  slots.  The  slots  can  have  the  same  or  different  sizes. Maximizing the number of items stored in a slot is similar to the 3D bin packing problem. This study proposes a heuristics algorithm to design the item's arrangement in a slot to optimize the slot's utilization. Furthermore, because there are many different slots and pods, the next problem is which item should be stored in which slot in which pod. This problem is a combinatorial problem.
Therefore, this study applies a metaheuristics approach to solve this problem. Regarding algorithm selection, we adopted GA and PSO, which have been widely used [20-23], as our methodologies.

This study aims to optimize pod utilization by maximizing the number of items stored in each slot  and  finding  the  best  item-slot-pod  arrangement.  This  study  combines  heuristics  and metaheuristics  algorithms  to  find  the  optimal  solution.  This  study  applies  two  metaheuristics algorithms: particle swarm optimization (PSO) and genetic algorithm (GA).

2. Limitations of Heuristic Approaches: Many studies employ heuristic methods to solve CLP,  but  these  methods  usually  can  only  find  approximate  solutions  rather  than  the optimal ones. Moreover, the effectiveness of these methods might vary depending on the specifics of the problem.
3. Lack of Experimental Data: Many studies might lack experimental data to validate their methods.  This  lack  of  data  could  be  due  to  difficulty  acquiring  real-world  packing problem data or because conducting experiments requires significant time and resources.

In  numerous  warehouses,  products  or  items  are  traditionally  stacked  on  shelves  in  an organized manner to facilitate retrieval, and personnel, often referred to as pickers, actively pick and pack these items according to specific customer orders. In situations with an intense flux of goods moving in and out of the warehouse, which is common in large-scale operations, Automated Storage/Retrieval Systems (AS/RS) are widely employed to streamline the process and enhance efficiency. However, this conventional warehouse automation method has limitations, including a rigid structure that makes altering inventory locations cumbersome, relatively high initial setup costs, and manual intervention in reallocating resources.

To combat these inherent challenges and to revolutionize the warehousing industry, Robotic Mobile  Fulfillment  Systems  (RMFS)  have  been  introduced  as  an  innovative  solution.  RMFS, characterized by its integration of cutting-edge robotics, is tailor-made for the unique demands of e-commerce warehouses. At the core of the RMFS is an automated parts-to-picker system. This system employs autonomous robots that tirelessly transport movable shelves, aptly termed 'pods,' to  and  fro  between storage areas and workstations. This system's ingenuity lies in eliminating walking time for pickers, which is achieved by having the pods brought directly to them. This process dramatically increases the picking rate, thereby enhancing overall productivity.

Within the workstations, there is a hive of activity where inventory is methodically placed onto the pods or diligently retrieved from them based on the requirements of the order at hand. Nevertheless,  implementing  RMFS  has  complexities  and  challenges    [24].  Notably,  logistical issues  include  the  strategic  assignment  of  customer  orders  to  workstations  and  the  efficient allocation of pods to storage locations [25]. These decision-making processes are not trivial and require intricate trade-offs to optimize the system. For instance, it might be logical to prioritize an order nearing its deadline by assigning it to a workstation. However, synergizing it with another order that shares a common aisle with the orders assigned to that workstation could lead to more efficient picking strategies. This condition might entail more picks per pod, reducing the trips each pod  needs  to  make,  culminating  in  enhanced  efficiency  and  resource  optimization.  The implementation of RMFS, therefore, necessitates careful planning and intelligent decision-making to harness its potential fully [26].

Based on past research [11, 27-29], there is a plethora of literature concerning the placement of SKUs in pods. Some studies have considered factors such as the association of SKU locations, the correlation in picking, batch processing, and the distance to move to other sites. Additionally, heuristic algorithms have been proposed to minimize inventory costs as much as possible. This study integrates the CLP with this issue and employs heuristic algorithms to enhance the efficiency of solving the problem.

The CLP is a geometric assignment challenge that entails loading a subset of rectangular items, often denoted as SKU (Stock Keeping Units), into a fixed-dimension rectangular container, such as pods. The aim is to maximize the volume of the packed boxes. The packing process has to satisfy an optimized objective function under two primary geometric feasibility prerequisites:
- Every small item must be completely contained within the large object, and
- There should be no overlapping among the smaller units.
CLP  are  diverse,  with  various  properties  constituting  their  characteristics.  They are traditionally categorized into two groups, as outlined by Wäscher and Haußner [13]. In the input minimization problem, the first category assumes sufficient storage space for all boxes. In such cases,  the  number of  containers  is  usually  non-restrictive,  with  the  primary  objective  being  to minimize the number of containers required to accommodate all boxes. Conversely, the second group,  the  output  maximization  problem,  operates  under  limited  container  space,  which  is insufficient for storing  all boxes. The aim here is to select a subset of boxes to maximize the volume or value of the load.

The classifications of cutting and packing problems proposed by Dyckhoff [30] and Wäscher, Haußner  [13]  offer  solid  foundations  for  investigations  in  this  field.  According  to  Wäscher, Haußner [13], these problems can be grouped based on dimensionality, the variety of large and small  items,  and  the  objective.  Within  the  scope  of  this  paper,  the  focus  is  primarily  on  3D rectangular items, with discussions on both single-bin and multi-bin packing problems.

The single-bin packing problem is a classic cutting and packing problem, where the objective is to place a set of items into the minimum number of bins of fixed dimensions. Each item has a certain volume or weight, while each bin has a maximum capacity. The challenge lies in allocating the items into the bins to maximize space utilization. Most of the literature concerning packing problems focuses on this type of problem, and there are various adaptations based on different problem  descriptions,  including  the  development  of  corresponding  mathematical  models  and algorithms (Phongmoo, Leksakul [31] and Araya, Guerrero [32])

The multi-bin packing problem extends the single-bin packing problem, where items can be divided into multiple categories or sets. Items from each set need to be packed into the same bin, and each bin can only contain items from a single set. Compared to the single-bin scenario, the multi-bin problem has received less attention. The objective is to satisfy the items' requirements with  the  minimum  number  of  containers.  In  past  literature,  Alonso  and  Alvarez-Valdes  [33] addressed this issue by minimizing the number of trucks used and solving it through an integer linear model while complying with certain constraints.
Ideally, we want to use the fewest shelves and have each slot filled as completely as possible. However, these two objectives may conflict in practice and must be balanced appropriately.

The CLP is a complex combinatorial problem. Research on it has been steadily increasing over the past decades. In most studies, heuristic or metaheuristic methods are applied to solve this problem, although exact algorithms are also available. Heuristic methods provide solutions quickly and are effective for problems demanding real-time decisions or when computational resources are limited. The simplicity of heuristics contributes to their accessibility and ease of understanding. However, these methods, designed specifically for a problem, may not always find the optimal solution, and their performance can significantly vary depending on the problem instance. Huang and Hwang [34] propose a heuristic algorithm for resolving the three-dimensional single-container loading problem through optimal placement. Owing to the NP-hard nature of the problem, it is framed  as  a  zero-one  mixed  integer  linear  programming  model.  The  suggested  heuristic  has demonstrated superior efficiency to the cutting-edge mixed integer linear program and pre-existing heuristic approaches. Gajda, Trivella [19] proposed Randomized Constructive Heuristic (RCH) algorithm  quickly  generates  superior  packing  solutions  and  effectively  addresses  a  logistics company's CPL.

On  the  other hand, exact algorithms  guarantee  solutions'  optimality,  given  enough computational time. They provide a reliable and precise way to benchmark the quality of heuristic and  metaheuristic  solutions.  However,  their  main  limitation  is  computational  inefficiency  for large-scale  problems  due  to  their  exhaustive  nature,  making  them  impractical  for  real-time decision-making or problems with large dimensions. Martello and Pisinger [35] offered an exact branch-and-bound  method  to  find  optimal  solutions  for  small-scale  instances  of  the  threedimensional bin packing problem (3D-BPP). Although exact algorithms ensure optimal solutions, their applicability is constrained for cases involving many boxes.

Metaheuristics, being more general, offer flexibility in application across various problem domains. They tend to explore a broader search space and can often provide good-quality solutions, even for complex problems. However, they require careful tuning of parameters for each problem, and  there  is  no  guarantee  of  finding  an  optimal  solution.  Kurpel  and  Scarpin  [17]  introduce mathematical models for various container loading problems, evaluate box placement techniques, and propose new methods to set boundaries for input minimization issues. It uses well-known datasets for computational experiments, often achieving new or improved optimal solutions.
Metaheuristics,  adaptable  to  various  problems,  have  also  been  employed  in  tackling  the Container  Loading  Problem  (CLP),  in  contrast  to  heuristics,  which  are  tailored  for  specific problems. Adapting these metaheuristics necessitates modifications to accommodate  the representation  of  CLP  solutions.  The  roster  of  employed  metaheuristics  encompasses  Genetic Algorithms (GA) [20-23], PSO, Artificial Bee Colony Optimization [36], Tabu Search [37], and Simulated Annealing, among others.

This study addresses a Single Large Object Placement Problem (SLOPP), striving to place small  items  (SKUs)  into  containers  (Pods).  Given  various  Pod  sizes,  this  study  utilizes  a metaheuristic approach to identify the most appropriate placement for each SKU. Ultimately, the objective is to fulfill the same amount of order requirements with the minimum number of shelves.

Metaheuristics have found significant applicability in Container Loading Problems (CLPs) due  to  their  flexibility,  adaptability,  and  effectiveness  in  handling  complex  combinatorial optimization  issues.  As  CLPs  are  NP-hard,  signifying  inherent  computational  complexity intensifying  with  problem  size,  finding  optimal  solutions  for  large-scale  problems  becomes challenging. This condition paves the way for heuristic and metaheuristic methods. With their high adaptability,  metaheuristics  can  accommodate  various  optimization  problems,  including  CLPs. Their stochastic processes help avoid premature convergence and encourage a broader solution to space  exploration.  Balancing  between  exploring  new  solution  areas  and  intensively  searching promising ones, they efficiently generate near-optimal solutions within reasonable timeframes. Although they do not guarantee an optimal solution, their delivery of high-quality solutions makes them crucial in efficiently solving CLPs.

This section discusses the research methodology of this study. In the first step, this study represents the problem as a mathematical model to get a better problem definition. Furthermore, as the problem can be divided into two main problems, the item-to-slot arrangement, and SKU-topod assignment problems, this study solves each problem with different approaches. The item-toslot arrangement problem is how to arrange the items into a slot so that the number of items stored in a slot can be maximized. This problem is similar to a 3D CLP. This study solves this problem with a heuristics approach. Figure 3.1 represents the flowchart of the execution process in this study.
Besides optimizing the item's arrangement in a slot, finding the best SKU-to-pod assignment is also crucial to minimize the number of pods. As this problem is a combinatorial problem, this study utilizes genetic algorithms and particle swarm optimization algorithms to find the best SKUto-pod assignment.

DBSCAN stands for Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise [38]. It is particularly valued for its capability to detect clusters of arbitrary shapes, based on the density of data points, without specifying the number of clusters beforehand.
The algorithm employs two parameters, eps representing the maximum distance between two data points to be considered neighbors and min\_samples, indicating the minimum number of points required to form a dense region. DBSCAN classifies points as core, border, or noise, with core points forming the clusters [38].
DBSCAN's ability to identify clusters of different shapes and handle noise efficiently has led to its widespread application in diverse fields like astronomy2 and bioinformatics [39]. However, the choice of parameters can significantly impact the results, and DBSCAN may struggle with clusters of varying densities.
This study will use this method to categorize thousands of SKUs (Stock Keeping Units) to reduce operational complexity. Moreover, items with large volumes are unlikely to be placed in the same pod. We have considered this issue and aim to distinguish SKUs through clustering.

The item-to-pod arrangement or assignment can be represented as an extension of 3D CLP. This study defines this problem's main objective as minimizing the number of pods that serve all demands. In order to minimize the number of pods, the utilization of each slot in each pod should be maximized. Therefore, the first problem represented in the mathematical model is the items' arrangement in a slot to maximize the slots' utilization.
This study adopts a 3D cartesian coordinate system, with the left-bottom-back vertex as the origin point, as shown in Figure 3.2. The items are arranged orthogonally within the container.

The second algorithm employed in this study is the PSO algorithm. While the GA algorithm represents the SKU-to-Pod assignment as a chromosome, PSO represents it as a particle with the same  configuration  as  the  chromosome.  Drawing  parallels  to  the  Genetic  Algorithm  (GA) principles,  each  particle  undergoes  updates  influenced  by  the  particle's  optimal  historical movement and the optimal movement observed within the entire swarm. Let P be a set of particles, 𝑃 = {𝑝1, 𝑝 2 , … , 𝑝 𝑁 } ,  where N is the number of particles. The set P denotes the position of the particles, 𝑉 = {𝑣1, 𝑣 2 , … , 𝑣 𝑁 } represents the velocity of each particle's movement, and the final position of a particle equates to the solution. With each iteration, particles are updated continuously according to Equations ( 3-18 ) and ( 3-19 ). The particles traverse the search space through the formula,  gravitating  toward  their  best  and  globally  optimal  solutions.  This  strategy  assists  the particles in evading local optima and converging towards the global optimum.

In the ever-changing landscape of consumer behavior, e-commerce entities find themselves in a state of perpetual evolution, constantly seeking advancements and improvements. Central to their mission is a dual objective - curbing process and demand costs while satisfying customer needs. A crucial element of this mission involves a logistical challenge: determining the optimal quantity of pods required within the constraints of limited warehouse space.
Therefore, to tackle this challenge, various strategies must be considered: effective placement of stock in slots, the appropriate designation of location for each Stock Keeping Unit (SKU), and many more. Our study embraces the reality of these operational complexities and contributes a proposed  solution.  By  leveraging  a  novel  3D-CLP  algorithm  and  harnessing  the  power  of metaheuristics, we have devised a solution tailored to these intricate real-world problems.
In the context of this study, it is noteworthy that our focus is on the 3D CLP. Attempting to express the complexities of this problem through a conventional mathematical model would prove overly complex and demand a significant time investment. To bypass these hurdles, we adopt a heuristic approach. Our strategy zeroes in on SKU placement in slots, aiming for optimal space utilization.

Building  on  this,  we  employ  a  sinlge  objective  heuristic  approach  to  discern  the  ideal placement for each SKU. We aim to reduce the number of pods required to meet our operational objectives.
The  experimental  results  underscore  the  considerable  impact  of  parameter  changes.  Our experiment incorporated six distinct scenarios, characterized by different levels of heterogeneity strong, medium, and weak - and differences in quantities, specifically low and high demand. The best average pod needed in these scenarios was quantified as 10.90, 30.10, 13.10, 39.40, 19.00, and 103.30, respectively, which all the best average results obtained by using PSO.
An interesting pattern emerged when comparing the performance of GA and PSO in these scenarios.  Despite  the  longer  time  commitment  necessitated  by  PSO,  it  consistently  yielded superior results. This result reinforces the merit of investing more time upfront to derive more efficient and optimal outcomes.

In the intricate realm of Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS), the dynamics of every operation hold paramount  significance. Each  action, whether latent or swift, can send reverberations throughout the system, instigating a chain reaction of effects on the subsequent tasks. In such a tightly-knit environment, even a slight deviation in one area can echo across the entire ecosystem, emphasizing the delicate interplay of components. A holistic approach becomes essential in a world where isolated solutions often fall short.
Our current study is grounded in real-world scenarios, drawing heavily from conditions typical to the Picking area. However, the breadth and depth of the RMFS world mean that our model, though  robust,  has  ample  room  for  expansion  and  further  fine-tuning.  The  more  nuances  we incorporate, the closer our model aligns with on-ground realities.

Stock allocation within the PODs  is far from a straightforward task.  Fundamental considerations, such as the weight-bearing capacity of each POD, must be juxtaposed against the collective endurance of the RMFS. It is a balancing act, ensuring we utilize the system to its fullest potential without overburdening it. Similarly, the strategic placement of stock is not just about space optimization but also about understanding the interrelationships between different Stock Keeping Units (SKUs). By analyzing buying patterns and SKU compatibility, we can create a layout where frequently co-purchased items are in proximity, streamlining retrieval processes and enhancing operational efficiency.
Central to our approach is the multi-objective heuristic algorithms, which, in their current form, represent just the tip of the iceberg. The possibilities are vast: from refining these algorithms to overhauling their architecture, every tweak can lead to substantial gains in computational speed. In doing so, we can pave the way for more agile, real-time solutions that resonate even more with the challenges of real-world RMFS. These enhancements can enrich the proposed model, bringing it closer to addressing the multifaceted challenges encountered in real-world RMFS.
